text: Monday, nine sharp.
Maya calls the help desk, a little upset.
Her ticket says closed, and nobody remembers closing it.
If the desk kept only the ticket's latest row, that's where the story would end.
Every update to that row was a small act of forgetting.
Act keeps the whole story instead, as events in one log.
Let's watch it remember.
At the left edge are the actors: people like Maya, and quiet helpers like the drain.
In the middle runs the Act app.
Every request knocks on one door, app dot do, then walks the action layer.
Below it live the slices: states with their actions and events, and the reactions and projections that answer them.
On the right is the event store.
One log, one dot per event, in the order things happened.
The stream a scene is about lights up.
Hover any dot, and its whole stream lights up with it.
Data travels along the link:
Maya opens a ticket, and its event lands at the end of the log.
Curious how something is built?
Its little code icon shows you, with links to read more.
The captions follow the voice, and the speed control next to Play sets the pace.
Play runs a chapter, the arrows step, and the menu jumps anywhere.
Ready?
Let's go.
Lee, the team lead, wants to know why one ticket took a whole week to close.
A table of current rows just shrugs.
A log can answer.
This is the desk's event store: every dot is one event, in the order it happened, wrapping like lines of text.
A ring is a snapshot, a square is a tombstone, and a hollow dot holds something sensitive.
The history grows from a fixed seed, so it's the same every time you watch.
Work keeps rolling in.
Each commit takes the next global id, so new events always land at the end.
Nothing already written ever changes.
Each event also belongs to one stream, and takes that stream's next version.
The dashed lens marks this scene's events, and the cells below zoom in.
Ticket 4821 holds version 0 and version 1, with other tickets chatting in between.
Reading one ticket's story is just a question asked of the same log.
Ask for the exact stream, and you get its events alone, in order.
Every event also remembers why it happened.
Its causation names the action and who did it.
Its correlation is a thread that ties a whole workflow together.
Maya's screen keeps flickering, and she'd like someone to care.
First the desk needs a ticket that knows what it is.
In Act that's a state: a Zod schema, a starting value, the events it emits, how each event patches it, and the actions that emit them.
Hand it to act, build, and you have an app.
Maya opens ticket 4830 with a title.
The first thing Act does is check her payload against the action's schema.
Then the action loads the stream.
Ticket 4830 is brand new, so it starts from its initial value, at version minus 1.
The handler decides what happened: a Ticket Opened, carrying her title.
The event folds into the state before anything is saved, and the result is checked against the schema.
The commit expects version minus 1, finds it, and lands as global id event 1905, stream version 0.
Maya gets back a snapshot for every event that landed.
She adds a message.
It loads version 0 and commits version 1, and the log grows by one, to event 1906.
Versions count within a stream; ids count across the whole store.
Later, loading the ticket replays those events in order.
The ticket was never saved as a row.
It's remembered.
Every desk has rules, and rules love to wander.
One hides in a controller, another in a service, and soon they disagree.
In Act every action walks the same checks, in the same order, and stops at the first one that fails.
Nothing is saved until the last one passes.
Maya tries to close her ticket with a reason of 42.
A number, where words belong.
The schema says no with a Validation Error, and the action never even loads.
Bo closes it properly, with a real reason.
Every check passes, and Ticket Closed lands as version 2.
Maya, still cross, tries to close it again.
A precondition is a named rule the action needs right now, and this ticket is no longer open.
The action politely refuses with a Precondition Error.
Some promises must hold after every action.
Those are invariants, and they live in the state's schema.
Say a buggy handler closes ticket 4822 without saying who closed it.
The schema spots the gap, and the action is refused with a Validation Error before anything is saved.
None of these refusals reached the log.
No event, no version, and no reaction woke up.
The log still ends at event 1907.
Two agents, one ticket, the very same instant.
Maya and Ana both add a message to ticket 4821, and both actions load it at version 1.
Maya is a hair faster, and her message lands as version 2 (event 1908).
Ana's commit expected 1 and found 2, so the store hands it back with a Concurrency Error.
It names the stream, the version she expected, and the one she found.
Nothing of hers was saved.
Give the action a retry budget, and Act handles the awkward part.
It reloads, checks the rules again on the fresh state, and commits.
Ana's message lands as version 3 (event 1909), and she never even knows there was a race.
When the caller pins a version, though, the conflict is final.
With an expected version of 1 the action fails at once.
No retry can make version 3 equal 1.
Ticket 4821 keeps growing, and replaying its whole life on every click would get slow.
A warm load starts from the cache, in memory by default, and replays only what came after.
Here the cache already holds the ticket at version 3, and nothing came after, so there's nothing to do.
With a snap rule on the state, an action that makes the rule true also saves a snapshot.
It's an event too, on the stream's next version (version 5, event 1911), holding the state at that moment.
Then the server restarts, and the cache is empty.
A cold load starts from the latest snapshot and folds only what came after, not the whole stream.
Sometimes the question is about the past.
A time-travel load reads only the events below event 1909, skipping the cache and any later snapshot, and it never writes a thing.
New tickets shouldn't sit around waiting to be noticed.
The desk wants each one assigned the moment it opens, without anyone wiring up a queue.
When an app with reactions starts, correlate reads the log from its bookmark and notes the work for every reaction.
Here it sweeps the whole store once.
After that, it only reads what's new.
Maya opens ticket 4831 (event 1912).
Its event has a reaction, so the commit schedules a settle all by itself.
No wiring, no message broker: the log is the backbone.
Correlate reads past its bookmark and asks each reaction where it should run.
The assign reaction names its own target stream for this ticket, which is subscribed, with work marked up to event 1912.
The drain claims targets that have work, each under a lease, and fetches the events past the target's watermark, which is minus 1 here.
The handler calls app dot do to assign the ticket.
That new action inherits the event that woke it: same correlation, with Ticket Opened as its cause.
On success the drain acks.
The watermark moves past event 1912, and the lease is released.
A stream is never acked past an event its reaction hasn't handled.
Settle keeps looping correlate and drain until a pass finds nothing.
The next pass reads event 1913, which no reaction wants, so the app is settled and says so.
Leave out the target, and a reaction runs on the event's own stream.
In tests, switch off auto-settle and walk the pipeline yourself, one step at a time.
Monday morning, and one worker can't keep up.
Two tickets open (event 1914, event 1915), and correlate marks two targets.
Two processes drain the same store and compete for the work.
Each claims a different target, because a lease someone holds is invisible to everyone else.
Then worker A trips over a cable mid-handler.
Its lease runs out, and exactly one other worker takes over.
B now runs both, and the failed try counts against the target's retry budget.
B's handlers assign both tickets (event 1916, event 1917), then ack both targets.
Nobody noticed a thing.
Some work is just slow, like calling another company's webhook.
It shouldn't hold up everything else.
A lane is a separate drain with its own lease and claim budget, so webhooks get a lane of their own, with 30-second leases.
Ticket 4832 escalates (event 1918).
The webhooks lane claims its target while the default lane keeps humming along.
Lanes run side by side, so the slow one never blocks the fast one.
Inside a lane, priority decides who gets picked first when work piles up.
It never reorders a stream's events, and it can change while the app runs.
Two in the morning, and the escalation service is down.
The webhook posts event 1918 and gets a 503 back.
A failed try waits out its backoff: 200 milliseconds for the first retry, times a jitter between 0.5 and 1.5.
The schedule lives on the target, so no worker jumps the gun.
Retries two and three fail too.
The wait doubles each time, to 400 milliseconds and then 800, up to a cap, each with its own jitter.
The fourth try fails, and the budget is spent, so the target blocks.
Claim skips it, its watermark waits just before event 1918, and a blocked event fires so a human can take a look.
By breakfast the service is back.
Unblocking picks up at the watermark: event 1918 goes out once more, and nothing before it runs again.
Ticket 4833 escalates (event 1919), and the service answers 400: a request that will never work, no matter how often you send it.
The webhook throws a Non Retryable Error, which blocks on the spot without spending the budget, unless blocking on errors is switched off.
Tempting as it is, this is not the moment for a reset.
Reset rewinds the watermark to minus 1 and replays everything, so every webhook would go out again.
Reset rebuilds; unblock recovers.
Sometimes it's the store itself that stumbles.
The drain, settle and autoclose loops share a circuit breaker: after enough failures it opens, leaves the store alone, and tries again after a cooldown.
An error event fires each time.
The store comes back, and the breaker closes on the next pass.
The bad request gets fixed upstream, and the operator unblocks the target.
A ticket nobody touches should escalate on its own, without a cron job sweeping the table at midnight.
Ticket 4821 is assigned to escalate after 10:00 (event 1920).
Correlate marks its escalate target, and the drain finds the reaction deferred: the event waits, and the target holds a due time.
Claim skips the target until 10:00.
The due time comes from the event, never from the clock on the wall, so a late worker lands on the same time.
At 10:00 it runs, and the ticket escalates (event 1921).
Ticket 4822 is set to escalate after 11:00 (event 1922), but Bo closes it at 10:40 (event 1923).
Nicely done, Bo.
At 11:00 the timer wakes up, loads the ticket, sees it's closed, and quietly goes back to sleep.
The drain acks, and nothing is added.
A guard like this is how a deferred chain ends.
When the wait depends on something the handler must look up first, it throws a Defer Signal instead.
That holds the stream until it's due, then delivers the event again.
Reactions that share a target travel as a group.
When one defers, the whole group waits and runs again when due.
A reaction that should wait alone gets a target of its own.
The support screen needs a list of tickets, fast.
Nobody wants to replay the log for every page view.
A state projection folds a state's own patches and writes one row per stream into a read model.
Its target is called tickets, and a new one starts at watermark minus 1.
It drains like any reaction: it catches up on the whole log, writes the rows, then acks.
If a write fails, the watermark stays put and nothing is lost.
Maya adds a message to ticket 4831 (event 1924), and the projection's next drain updates a single row.
A slice bundles partial states, projections and reactions into one feature.
Partial states with the same name merge into one, so features grow without stepping on each other's toes.
Then the screen gets a redesign, and the table needs a new shape.
Empty it and reset the projection.
The watermark goes back to minus 1, and the replay schedules itself.
The replay walks the log again from event 1819, and the rows come back, good as new.
Nothing in the log changed.
A projection is only a view of it.
An agent can juggle five open tickets at most, and that rule belongs to the agent, not the ticket.
So assigning one touches both.
On a fresh store, with two agents and Bo already at five, Lee assigns ticket 5200 to Ana.
The action loads every state the decision needs, all at once.
The ticket has no agent yet, so that load is skipped.
Each event goes to the stream that asked for it: the assignment to the ticket, and the taken slot to Ana.
The dropped one goes away with the skipped load.
Both land in one commit, each stream guarded by the version it had at load.
All or nothing.
Next, Lee tries to give ticket 5201 to Bo.
That would make 6 open tickets for Bo, and his state's schema says no.
It's a Validation Error, and nothing lands on any stream.
So Lee gives 5201 to Ana instead, loading her stream at version 1.
Meanwhile ticket 5200 closes, and closing frees Ana's slot in its own commit.
Her stream moves to version 2.
Lee's commit expected Ana at version 1 and found version 2, so the whole commit bounces with a Concurrency Error that names her stream.
The retry budget reloads every stream and decides again.
The retry sees Ana with 0 open tickets and commits both events.
A load that lists no events is just a read: nothing is added to it, so it isn't guarded.
A customer writes in: please forget me.
In a log that never forgets, that sounds impossible, unless the personal bits were kept apart from the start.
Lee registers, and his email is marked sensitive, so it never goes into the event's data.
It goes into a separate pii column of the same row, in the same transaction.
A read with no actor, like a background job or a script, sees REDACTED where every sensitive field would be.
Reactions and projections never see them either.
The state's disclose rule decides who may read the real thing.
Lee loads his own stream as himself, the rule agrees, and he sees his email.
Then Lee asks to be forgotten.
Forgetting user 42 wipes the pii column of every event on the stream, right where it sits.
Every later read gets SHREDDED, even for the boss.
Everything else in the log stays.
A snapshot would copy that data somewhere forget can't reach, so a state with sensitive fields can't snap, and the build says so.
For the same reason, a restart close skips such a stream.
A year later, closed tickets still sit in the log, taking up space and slowing every scan.
Time to close the books, carefully.
Ticket 4822 is done, but the tickets projection has only read up to event 1615, so the stream is skipped for now.
A close never drops events a reaction hasn't seen.
The projection catches up, and close tries again.
It commits a tombstone guard at the stream's version (event 1618, version 3).
From here on, nobody can write to it.
The archive callback runs while the stream is guarded.
If it fails, the stream stays guarded and nothing is deleted, so the close can simply try again.
Then the stream's events are deleted in one transaction, leaving a single seed: a tombstone at version 0 (event 1619).
The cache is updated, and a closed event fires.
Any action on a closed stream now gets a Stream Closed Error.
The tombstone is its final word.
A restart is the gentler close.
Ana's stream is guarded and deleted, then seeded with a snapshot of her final state at version 0 (event 1621).
Her next action lands on version 1 (event 1622), picking up right where the seed left off.
The log gets lighter, and the state carries on.
At scale the same dance runs stream by stream: check for pending work, guard, archive, delete, and leave one tombstone at version 0.
The dots lift away into the archive, leaving holes, and the seeds land at the end.
The ids of deleted events are never reused, so the holes stay until a restore tidies up.
The counts in the store's header always come from the store itself.
Nobody wants to remember to close tickets by hand, months after they're done.
An autoclose rule becomes a reaction on the state's events, one target per stream.
Ticket 7001 closed on Feb 20, so the reaction waits 90 days: a stored schedule, with no sweep.
When it comes due, inside the quiet off-hours window, it checks the live head.
Still closed, so it runs the same close an operator would, archiving through the state's own archive.
A reopened ticket would be left alone.
There's no sweep job anywhere.
Each stream's own timer comes due by itself, and each close runs only when that ticket is still closed and old enough.
Here the ones due by day 210, a day picked for the example, retire together.
Some streams never end.
A ledger keeps taking entries for years, and its oldest history just costs space.
Keeping 180 days trims anything older.
Say today is Oct 1 (the dates here are picked for the example), so the cutoff is Apr 4.
The closest snapshot before that is from Mar 01 (event 1577).
A windowed close deletes only the events below that snapshot.
No tombstone and no seed: the snapshot holds the balance, and the ledger keeps going.
The window moves forward as the ledger commits.
A ledger that went quiet gets trimmed with an explicit windowed close, which archives only through its own archive.
Every ledger plays by the same rule: find the closest snapshot older than the cutoff (day 180 here, picked for the example) and delete only what's below it.
A ledger without one keeps everything.
The snapshots stay, and every ledger stays live.
After all that closing and trimming, the store looks like Swiss cheese, and an old event name is still hanging around.
Restore copies a source into a sink in one transaction.
Ids renumber neatly, created times are kept, and causation follows the new ids.
It can tidy up on the way, dropping every snapshot that has history before it, while keeping a stream's first one, the one a trimmed or restarted stream starts from.
It can update old events too.
On the live store an event never changes, and a new name like Posted version 2 takes over from the old one.
A restore can rewrite the old ones as they pass, checked on both sides.
Restore leaves the cache and your read models alone.
So after a big restore, clear the cache and rebuild the projections with a reset.
And before trouble finds you, an audit walks the store and tells the operator what needs attention:
schema drift, close and restart candidates, stuck reactions, snapshot drift and correlation gaps.
The desk grows to two servers sharing one Postgres store, and each wants to know when the other writes.
Without notify, server B only notices A's commit when it polls, every 10 s by default.
With a store that notifies, A's commit taps B on the shoulder right away, and B settles.
A server never hears its own commits, since those already settle locally.
Inject the store before building the app, or nothing gets wired.
Notify is a nudge, not a promise.
Correctness always comes from claiming and draining over the store, which is why the wake-up channel can be swapped, for example for Redis.
One process can also host several Acts, each with its own store and cache, passed in together.
Two tenants, two logs, and no gossip between them.
One store always belongs to one application.
When it's time to go home, shutdown waits for in-flight drains up to a grace period, hands back the correlation lease, and starts nothing new.
Agents don't type app dot do; they click buttons in a browser.
The HTTP package walks the registry and builds a route for every action: the payload goes in, its snapshots come out, typed all the way to the browser.
Errors map to status codes in one table, so a refused precondition comes back as 409 with PRECONDITION.
With server-sent events, every committed change reaches the browsers watching that state as a small, versioned patch.
A browser that falls behind knows to refetch.
Calls to the outside world are reactions too.
A webhook handler comes with a timeout, an idempotency key taken from the event id, and typed errors that drive retries and blocking.
Everything you've watched ran on one port: the store.
In-memory is the default, and Postgres and SQLite run the very same log in production.
Inject one before building the app.
Swap the adapter, and nothing above the log changes: same ids, same versions, same leases.
A new adapter earns its badge with the TCK, the same test suite the built-in stores run.
A commit across streams is all or nothing, a live lease belongs to one worker, a truncate leaves a seed, and notify never echoes.
The rules a store must follow are exported from the adapter entry point, so every store refuses the same bad writes and plants the same seeds.
And that's the tour: every capability you saw is something the log does.
